Chapter 3: Defining the Problem – Finding the Root Cause

Introduction: Turning Insights into Focus

Welcome, high schoolers, to Chapter 3 of your Design Thinking adventure! After diving deep into empathy in Chapter 2 and learning how to understand others’ needs, it’s time to take all those observations, stories, and insights and transform them into something actionable. This chapter is all about Defining the Problem—the second stage of Design Thinking—where we shift from simply noticing issues to pinpointing the root causes and framing them in a way that sparks creative solutions.

Defining the problem is like setting up the target before you shoot an arrow. If your target is unclear or off-center, your solutions won’t hit the mark, no matter how brilliant they are. In this chapter, we’ll guide you through the process of moving from vague observations to focused problem statements that drive real change. You’ll learn how to ask powerful questions like “Why?” and “How Might We?”, narrow down broad issues into specific challenges, avoid jumping to conclusions by validating your ideas with peers, and write clear, user-centered problem statements. Whether you’re tackling a school issue, a community challenge, or a personal project, mastering this stage ensures you’re solving the right problem for the right people. So, let’s sharpen our focus and get ready to define problems that matter!

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content:
Chapter 3: Defining the Problem – Finding the Root Cause

 

 

Section 1- Moving from Observations to Problem Statements

Let’s start by understanding what it means to move from observations to problem statements—a critical first step in the Define stage of Design Thinking. In Chapter 2, you gathered a ton of information through empathy tools like interviews, surveys, and observation, along with activities like role-playing and empathy maps. You’ve likely collected stories, pain points, and insights about what people are experiencing. Now, it’s time to make sense of all that data and turn it into a clear direction for your project.

What’s the Difference?

  • Observations are raw data—things you’ve seen, heard, or noted about users. For example, “Students are frustrated waiting for the school bus because it’s often late.” These are facts or feelings straight from your empathy work.
  • Problem Statements are concise summaries of the core issue, framed in a way that focuses on the user’s need and sets up a path for solutions. For the same observation, a problem statement might be: “Students need a reliable way to get to school on time because late buses cause stress and missed classes.”

    •  

Why This Transition Matters: Turning observations into problem statements helps you move from simply knowing there’s an issue to understanding what specifically needs to be addressed. It’s like going from saying, “Something’s wrong,” to “Here’s exactly what we need to fix and for whom.” This step ensures you’re not just reacting to surface-level complaints but digging into a meaningful challenge. As a high schooler, this skill can help with anything from group projects (like figuring out why teamwork isn’t clicking) to personal goals (like why you’re struggling to stay organized).

 

How to Move from Observations to Problem Statements:

  • Review Your Empathy Data: Look back at your notes, empathy maps, and pain points from Chapter 2. Highlight key themes or recurring issues. For instance, if multiple students mention stress about late buses, that’s a pattern to focus on.
  • Identify the User: Who is most affected by this issue? Be specific—don’t just say “students,” but “freshmen who rely on the school bus to get to morning classes.”
  • Pinpoint the Need: What does this user need to improve their situation? Focus on their core struggle, like “needing a predictable schedule to avoid stress.”
  • Frame the Challenge: Combine the user and their need into a short statement that suggests there’s a problem to solve. Avoid solutions for now—just state the issue, like “Freshmen need a predictable bus schedule to avoid stress from being late to class.”
  • Stay User-Centered: Always keep the focus on the person experiencing the problem, not on what you think should happen. This keeps your work grounded in empathy.

    •  

Example in Action:

  • Observation: “I noticed during lunch that some students sit alone and look uncomfortable while others chat in big groups.”
  • Problem Statement: “Some students need a way to feel included during lunch because sitting alone makes them feel isolated.” This shift from observation to problem statement clarifies who is affected (some students), what they need (to feel included), and why it matters (isolation feels bad).

    •  

Activity for Practice: Grab a piece of paper and think of one observation from your school or community (like something you’ve noticed in the cafeteria, hallways, or a local park). Write it down as a raw observation. Then, turn it into a problem statement by identifying the user, their need, and why it’s important. Share it with a classmate to see if it’s clear and focused on the right person.

By moving from observations to problem statements, you’re setting the stage for the rest of the Define process. You’re not just collecting random complaints—you’re starting to shape a target that’s worth solving. This is your first step toward making a real impact!

 

 

Section 2- Asking “Why” and “How Might We” Questions

Now that you’ve started framing problem statements, let’s dive into two powerful questioning techniques that help you dig deeper into the root cause of an issue and open the door to creative thinking: asking “Why?” and “How Might We?” (HMW). These questions are like tools in your Design Thinking toolbox—they help you uncover hidden layers of a problem and reframe challenges in a way that invites solutions. As a high school student, mastering these questions will not only help with projects but also teach you how to approach any problem with curiosity and optimism.

 

  • 1. Asking “Why?” – Uncovering the Root Cause: The “Why?” technique is all about peeling back the layers of a problem to understand its deeper cause. Often, what seems like the issue on the surface isn’t the real problem—it’s just a symptom of something bigger. Asking “Why?” multiple times (often called the “5 Whys” method) helps you drill down to the root.
  • How It Works: Start with an observation or initial problem statement. Ask “Why?” to explain it. Then, ask “Why?” again about your answer. Repeat this 3-5 times until you feel you’ve hit a fundamental reason.
  • Example: Let’s say your observation is “Students are often late to first period.”
    • Why? “Because the school bus arrives late.”
    • Why? “Because the bus route has too many stops.”
    • Why? “Because the school district hasn’t updated routes to account for new neighborhoods.”
    • Why? “Because there’s no system to review bus routes regularly.”
    • Root Cause: The real problem isn’t just late buses—it’s the lack of a system to update routes.
  • Why It Matters: Getting to the root cause prevents you from solving the wrong problem. If you stopped at “late buses,” you might just add more buses, which could be costly and ineffective if the route system is the real issue.
  • Tip for High Schoolers: Use “Why?” in group discussions or even personal reflection. It’s great for understanding why a club isn’t popular, why homework feels overwhelming, or why a friend seems upset.

    •  

  • 2. Asking “How Might We?” – Framing for Solutions: Once you’ve dug into the “Why,” the “How Might We?” (HMW) question helps you reframe the problem as an opportunity for innovation. HMW questions are optimistic, action-oriented, and invite brainstorming by focusing on possibilities rather than limitations.
  • How It Works: Take your problem statement or root cause and turn it into a question starting with “How might we…?” Make sure it’s specific enough to guide ideas but broad enough to allow creativity.
  • Example: Using the bus issue:
    • Problem Statement: “Freshmen need a predictable bus schedule to avoid stress from being late.”
    • HMW Question: “How might we create a reliable bus schedule for freshmen so they arrive at school on time without stress?”
  • Why It Matters: HMW questions shift your mindset from “This is a problem” to “Let’s solve this together!” They’re especially useful in team settings because they encourage everyone to contribute ideas without fear of criticism.
  • Tip for High Schoolers: Write a few HMW questions for any challenge you face, whether it’s school-related or personal. For example, “How might we make study groups more fun so everyone shows up?” It’s a great way to kickstart creative thinking.

    •  

Combining “Why” and “HMW”: Use “Why?” to dig deep, then “HMW” to pivot toward action. For instance, after discovering the root cause of late buses is outdated routes, you might ask, “How might we design a system to regularly update bus routes so students arrive on time?” This combo ensures you’re solving the real issue in a forward-thinking way.

 

Activity for Practice: Pick a school or community issue (like crowded hallways or limited after-school activities). Write down the surface problem, then use the “5 Whys” to find a root cause. Once you’ve got it, turn it into an HMW question. Example: Surface Problem: “Hallways are too crowded between classes.” Why? (Ask 5 times to dig deeper.) HMW: “How might we manage hallway traffic so students can get to class without stress?” Share your HMW question with a friend for feedback.

Asking “Why?” and “How Might We?” are game-changers in Design Thinking. They help you avoid quick fixes and instead focus on meaningful, innovative solutions. Keep these questions in your back pocket—they’re tools you can use for any challenge life throws at you!

 

Section 3- Narrowing Down Issues to Actionable Challenges

At this point, you’ve gathered insights, framed initial problem statements, and dug deeper with “Why?” and “How Might We?” questions. But sometimes, the problems you uncover can feel overwhelming or too broad to tackle. That’s where narrowing down issues to actionable challenges comes in. This step is about taking big, vague problems and focusing on specific, manageable pieces that you can realistically address. As a high schooler, this skill will help you break down complex issues—whether it’s a school project or a personal goal—into something you can actually work on.

 

Why Narrowing Down Matters: Broad problems like “The school cafeteria is a mess” or “Teens in my community are bored” are hard to solve because they’re too general. They include many smaller issues, and trying to fix everything at once can leave you stuck. Narrowing down helps you zoom in on one specific aspect of the problem that’s both important to users and doable for you to tackle. It turns a giant mountain into a climbable hill.

 

How to Narrow Down Issues: Here’s a step-by-step guide to focus your problem into an actionable challenge:

  • List All Related Issues: Start with your broad problem and brainstorm all the smaller issues or pain points connected to it. For example, if the broad problem is “The school cafeteria is a mess,” smaller issues might include long lines, not enough seating, unhealthy food options, and trash everywhere.
  • Prioritize Based on Impact: Look at your list and think about which issue affects the most people or causes the most frustration. Use your empathy data from Chapter 2—did students mention long lines the most in surveys? Does not having enough seats lead to the strongest emotions? Pick the one with the biggest impact.
  • Consider Feasibility: Think about what you can realistically address given your time, resources, and skills as a high school student. Solving unhealthy food options might require big changes to school policy (hard to do quickly), but addressing long lines might be something you can brainstorm solutions for now.
  • Reframe as a Specific Challenge: Take the narrowed-down issue and turn it into a focused problem statement or HMW question. For long lines, you might say, “Students need a faster way to get through cafeteria lines during lunch because waiting cuts into their break time.”
  • Check with Users: If possible, ask a few people (like classmates) if this specific challenge resonates with them. Does it match their experience? This ensures you’re not narrowing down to something irrelevant.

    •  

Example in Action:

  • Broad Problem: “Teens in my community have nothing to do after school.”
  • List of Issues: No safe hangout spots, expensive activities, lack of teen-friendly events, no transportation to existing programs.
  • Prioritize by Impact: Surveys show most teens mention “no safe hangout spots” as their biggest frustration because they feel bored or unsafe wandering around.
  • Consider Feasibility: Creating a new community center might be too big, but finding an existing space (like a library) for teen hangouts feels doable.
  • Specific Challenge: “How might we create a safe after-school hangout spot for teens in the community library so they have a place to relax without cost?”

    •  

Activity for Practice: Think of a broad issue at your school or in your community (like “School events aren’t well-attended” or “My neighbourhood isn’t teen-friendly”). Write down the broad problem, then list 3-5 smaller issues connected to it. Pick one based on impact and feasibility, and reframe it as a specific HMW question or problem statement. Discuss with a partner to see if they agree with your focus.

Narrowing down turns overwhelming problems into actionable challenges you can actually tackle. It’s about working smarter, not harder—focusing your energy on a piece of the puzzle that makes a real difference. This step keeps your Design Thinking project moving forward without getting bogged down by “too much to fix.”

 

 

Section 4- Avoiding Assumptions: Validating Problems with Peers

As you narrow down your problem and start shaping a clear focus, there’s a sneaky trap to watch out for: assumptions. Assumptions are ideas or beliefs you hold about a problem or user without checking if they’re true. While your empathy work in Chapter 2 helps ground you in real user needs, it’s easy to accidentally fill in gaps with what you think is happening instead of what’s actually happening. That’s why validating problems with peers is a crucial step in the Define stage. As a high school student, this process teaches you to double-check your ideas and stay open to feedback—skills that are awesome for teamwork and problem-solving in any area of life.

 

Why Assumptions Can Be Dangerous: Assumptions can lead you to define the wrong problem or focus on something that doesn’t actually matter to users. For example, you might assume that students skip school events because they’re “boring,” so you focus on making them flashier. But if you don’t check, you might miss that the real reason is timing—events are scheduled when many students have after-school jobs. Solving for “boring” won’t fix the attendance issue. Validating helps ensure you’re on the right track.

 

How Assumptions Sneak In:

  • Personal Bias: You might think everyone feels the same way you do. If you don’t mind long cafeteria lines, you might assume others don’t either.
  • Limited Data: If you only interviewed two people, you might overgeneralize their opinions to everyone.
  • Jumping to Solutions: Sometimes, you get excited about a cool idea (like a new app for bus schedules) and assume the problem must fit that solution, instead of checking if it’s the real need.

    •  

How to Validate Problems with Peers: Validating means testing your problem statement or HMW question with others to see if it matches their experiences. Here’s how to do it:

  • Share Your Problem Statement: Write down your focused problem or HMW question. For example, “How might we speed up cafeteria lines so students have more time to eat during lunch?”
  • Ask a Small Group of Peers: Talk to 3-5 classmates, friends, or others who are part of the user group (or know the issue). Keep it casual—say, “I’m working on a project and want your thoughts. Does this problem feel real to you?”
  • Ask Specific Questions: Don’t just ask, “Do you agree?” Dig deeper with:
    • “Have you experienced this issue yourself? Can you tell me about it?”
    • “Is this the biggest frustration for you, or is there something else?”
    • “Does this problem statement capture what you’re feeling?”
  • Listen Without Defending: If they disagree or point out something new, don’t argue—listen. Their feedback might show you’ve made an assumption or missed a key pain point.
  • Adjust if Needed: If multiple peers say the problem isn’t quite right, revisit your empathy data or ask more “Why?” questions to refine it. For instance, if they say long lines aren’t the issue but messy payment systems are, update your focus.

    •  

Example in Action:

  • Initial Problem Statement: “Students need quieter study spaces in the library because noise makes it hard to focus.”
  • Validation with Peers: You ask five classmates. Three say noise isn’t a big deal—they wear headphones. Two mention the real issue is not enough tables during finals.
  • Adjustment: Based on feedback, you revise to: “How might we provide more study tables in the library during finals so students have space to work?” This pivot ensures you’re solving a real, shared problem, not an assumed one.

Activity for Practice: Take your narrowed-down problem statement or HMW question from the last section. Share it with at least two friends or classmates. Ask them if it feels like a real issue and if there’s anything you’re missing. Write down their feedback and note if you need to adjust your problem focus. Example: If your HMW is about hallway crowding and they say the bigger issue is locker placement, consider tweaking your statement.

Avoiding assumptions by validating with peers keeps your Design Thinking process honest and user-centered. It’s a quick reality check that saves you from wasting time on the wrong problem. Plus, it builds collaboration skills—asking for input shows you value others’ perspectives, which is huge in school and beyond!

 

Section 5- Writing Clear and Specific Problem Statements

You’ve gathered insights, dug into root causes, narrowed your focus, and validated your ideas. Now, it’s time to lock in your direction by writing clear and specific problem statements. A problem statement is the final output of the Define stage in Design Thinking—it’s a short, focused summary of the challenge you’re tackling, centered on the user’s needs. Getting this right is crucial because it guides the rest of your project through ideation, prototyping, and testing. As a high schooler, learning to write strong problem statements will help you clarify goals for anything from class assignments to personal initiatives.

What Makes a Good Problem Statement? A great problem statement is:

  • User-Centered: It focuses on who is affected and their specific need, not on a solution or your opinion.
  • Clear: It’s easy to understand, with no vague or confusing language.
  • Specific: It pinpoints a particular challenge, not a broad or general issue.
  • Actionable: It suggests a need or opportunity that can be addressed through design or innovation.
  • Empathy-Driven: It reflects the real feelings, struggles, or goals of the user, based on your Chapter 2 work.

    •  

Structure of a Problem Statement: A simple and effective format for writing problem statements is: [User Group] needs [specific need or goal] because [reason or impact of the problem].

  • User Group: Who is affected? Be specific (e.g., “high school sophomores” not just “students”).
  • Specific Need or Goal: What do they need to improve their situation? Focus on the core issue.
  • Reason or Impact: Why does this matter? Connect to their emotions or consequences.

    •  

How to Write a Clear and Specific Problem Statement: Follow these steps to craft your statement:

  • Start with Your User: Use your empathy data and validation feedback to name the specific group you’re designing for. Example: “High school athletes.”
  • Define Their Need: Look at your narrowed-down challenge or HMW question. What do they need to make their experience better? Example: “Need a better way to store gear.”
  • Explain the ‘Because’: Tie the need to a real impact or emotion from your insights. Example: “Because small lockers cause frustration and lost time before practice.”
  • Put It Together: Combine into one sentence: “High school athletes need a better way to store gear because small lockers cause frustration and lost time before practice.”
  • Test for Clarity: Read it aloud or share it with someone. Does it make sense? Is it focused? If it feels too broad or vague, refine it. Avoid solutions (like “need bigger lockers”)—focus on the need, not the fix.

    •  

Examples of Good vs. Weak Problem Statements:

  • Weak: “The school needs to fix the lockers.” (Not user-centered, too vague, suggests a solution.)
  • Good: “High school athletes need more accessible storage for sports gear because cramped lockers delay them before practice and cause stress.” (Specific user, clear need, impactful reason.)
  • Weak: “Students don’t like the cafeteria.” (Too broad, no specific need or reason.)
  • Good: “Freshmen need a quicker way to pay for lunch in the cafeteria because long lines mean they miss out on eating time and feel rushed.” (Focused user, actionable need, clear impact.)

    •  

Common Mistakes to Avoid:

  • Being Too Broad: “Everyone at school has problems” doesn’t help you focus. Narrow it to a specific group and issue.
  • Including Solutions: Don’t say “need a new app” or “need more buses.” Stick to the need, not how to solve it (that’s for the next stage).
  • Ignoring the User: Don’t write from your perspective (“I think we should…”). Center the user’s experience.
  • Skipping the ‘Why’: Without a reason, the statement lacks emotional weight. Always connect to impact or feelings.

Activity for Practice: Think of the narrowed-down challenge you’ve been working on (or pick a new school/community issue). Write a problem statement using the format: “[User Group] needs [specific need or goal] because [reason or impact].” Then, check it against the criteria (user-centered, clear, specific, actionable, empathy-driven). Swap with a classmate and give each other feedback—does it make sense? Is it focused enough?

Writing clear and specific problem statements is the capstone of the Define stage. It’s your North Star for the rest of the Design Thinking process, ensuring every idea and prototype you create later is aimed at solving a real, meaningful challenge. Plus, this skill helps you communicate ideas effectively—whether you’re pitching a project to a teacher or explaining a goal to a friend.

 

Chapter Wrap-up

Great job, everyone, on completing Chapter 3: Defining the Problem! You’ve taken a huge leap forward in your Design Thinking journey by learning how to transform raw observations and empathy insights into focused, actionable challenges. You’ve explored how to move from vague issues to problem statements, dug deep with “Why?” and “How Might We?” questions, narrowed broad problems into specific targets, avoided assumptions by validating with peers, and crafted clear, user-centered problem statements.

Defining the problem isn’t just about naming what’s wrong—it’s about understanding the root cause and setting up a clear path for creative solutions. The skills you’ve built here, like asking powerful questions and seeking feedback, are tools you can use in school projects, personal goals, and beyond. You’re now ready to move into the next stage of Design Thinking: Ideation, where you’ll brainstorm wild and wonderful ways to solve the problem you’ve defined. Keep your problem statement close—it’s your guide as we dive into generating ideas in Chapter 4. You’re doing fantastic—let’s keep the momentum going!

Chapter 3: Defining the Problem – Finding the Root Cause

 

 

Section 1- Moving from Observations to Problem Statements

Let’s start by understanding what it means to move from observations to problem statements—a critical first step in the Define stage of Design Thinking. In Chapter 2, you gathered a ton of information through empathy tools like interviews, surveys, and observation, along with activities like role-playing and empathy maps. You’ve likely collected stories, pain points, and insights about what people are experiencing. Now, it’s time to make sense of all that data and turn it into a clear direction for your project.

What’s the Difference?

  • Observations are raw data—things you’ve seen, heard, or noted about users. For example, “Students are frustrated waiting for the school bus because it’s often late.” These are facts or feelings straight from your empathy work.
  • Problem Statements are concise summaries of the core issue, framed in a way that focuses on the user’s need and sets up a path for solutions. For the same observation, a problem statement might be: “Students need a reliable way to get to school on time because late buses cause stress and missed classes.”

    •  

Why This Transition Matters: Turning observations into problem statements helps you move from simply knowing there’s an issue to understanding what specifically needs to be addressed. It’s like going from saying, “Something’s wrong,” to “Here’s exactly what we need to fix and for whom.” This step ensures you’re not just reacting to surface-level complaints but digging into a meaningful challenge. As a high schooler, this skill can help with anything from group projects (like figuring out why teamwork isn’t clicking) to personal goals (like why you’re struggling to stay organized).

 

How to Move from Observations to Problem Statements:

  • Review Your Empathy Data: Look back at your notes, empathy maps, and pain points from Chapter 2. Highlight key themes or recurring issues. For instance, if multiple students mention stress about late buses, that’s a pattern to focus on.
  • Identify the User: Who is most affected by this issue? Be specific—don’t just say “students,” but “freshmen who rely on the school bus to get to morning classes.”
  • Pinpoint the Need: What does this user need to improve their situation? Focus on their core struggle, like “needing a predictable schedule to avoid stress.”
  • Frame the Challenge: Combine the user and their need into a short statement that suggests there’s a problem to solve. Avoid solutions for now—just state the issue, like “Freshmen need a predictable bus schedule to avoid stress from being late to class.”
  • Stay User-Centered: Always keep the focus on the person experiencing the problem, not on what you think should happen. This keeps your work grounded in empathy.

    •  

Example in Action:

  • Observation: “I noticed during lunch that some students sit alone and look uncomfortable while others chat in big groups.”
  • Problem Statement: “Some students need a way to feel included during lunch because sitting alone makes them feel isolated.” This shift from observation to problem statement clarifies who is affected (some students), what they need (to feel included), and why it matters (isolation feels bad).

    •  

Activity for Practice: Grab a piece of paper and think of one observation from your school or community (like something you’ve noticed in the cafeteria, hallways, or a local park). Write it down as a raw observation. Then, turn it into a problem statement by identifying the user, their need, and why it’s important. Share it with a classmate to see if it’s clear and focused on the right person.

By moving from observations to problem statements, you’re setting the stage for the rest of the Define process. You’re not just collecting random complaints—you’re starting to shape a target that’s worth solving. This is your first step toward making a real impact!

 

 

Section 2- Asking “Why” and “How Might We” Questions

Now that you’ve started framing problem statements, let’s dive into two powerful questioning techniques that help you dig deeper into the root cause of an issue and open the door to creative thinking: asking “Why?” and “How Might We?” (HMW). These questions are like tools in your Design Thinking toolbox—they help you uncover hidden layers of a problem and reframe challenges in a way that invites solutions. As a high school student, mastering these questions will not only help with projects but also teach you how to approach any problem with curiosity and optimism.

 

  • 1. Asking “Why?” – Uncovering the Root Cause: The “Why?” technique is all about peeling back the layers of a problem to understand its deeper cause. Often, what seems like the issue on the surface isn’t the real problem—it’s just a symptom of something bigger. Asking “Why?” multiple times (often called the “5 Whys” method) helps you drill down to the root.
  • How It Works: Start with an observation or initial problem statement. Ask “Why?” to explain it. Then, ask “Why?” again about your answer. Repeat this 3-5 times until you feel you’ve hit a fundamental reason.
  • Example: Let’s say your observation is “Students are often late to first period.”
    • Why? “Because the school bus arrives late.”
    • Why? “Because the bus route has too many stops.”
    • Why? “Because the school district hasn’t updated routes to account for new neighborhoods.”
    • Why? “Because there’s no system to review bus routes regularly.”
    • Root Cause: The real problem isn’t just late buses—it’s the lack of a system to update routes.
  • Why It Matters: Getting to the root cause prevents you from solving the wrong problem. If you stopped at “late buses,” you might just add more buses, which could be costly and ineffective if the route system is the real issue.
  • Tip for High Schoolers: Use “Why?” in group discussions or even personal reflection. It’s great for understanding why a club isn’t popular, why homework feels overwhelming, or why a friend seems upset.

    •  

  • 2. Asking “How Might We?” – Framing for Solutions: Once you’ve dug into the “Why,” the “How Might We?” (HMW) question helps you reframe the problem as an opportunity for innovation. HMW questions are optimistic, action-oriented, and invite brainstorming by focusing on possibilities rather than limitations.
  • How It Works: Take your problem statement or root cause and turn it into a question starting with “How might we…?” Make sure it’s specific enough to guide ideas but broad enough to allow creativity.
  • Example: Using the bus issue:
    • Problem Statement: “Freshmen need a predictable bus schedule to avoid stress from being late.”
    • HMW Question: “How might we create a reliable bus schedule for freshmen so they arrive at school on time without stress?”
  • Why It Matters: HMW questions shift your mindset from “This is a problem” to “Let’s solve this together!” They’re especially useful in team settings because they encourage everyone to contribute ideas without fear of criticism.
  • Tip for High Schoolers: Write a few HMW questions for any challenge you face, whether it’s school-related or personal. For example, “How might we make study groups more fun so everyone shows up?” It’s a great way to kickstart creative thinking.

    •  

Combining “Why” and “HMW”: Use “Why?” to dig deep, then “HMW” to pivot toward action. For instance, after discovering the root cause of late buses is outdated routes, you might ask, “How might we design a system to regularly update bus routes so students arrive on time?” This combo ensures you’re solving the real issue in a forward-thinking way.

 

Activity for Practice: Pick a school or community issue (like crowded hallways or limited after-school activities). Write down the surface problem, then use the “5 Whys” to find a root cause. Once you’ve got it, turn it into an HMW question. Example: Surface Problem: “Hallways are too crowded between classes.” Why? (Ask 5 times to dig deeper.) HMW: “How might we manage hallway traffic so students can get to class without stress?” Share your HMW question with a friend for feedback.

Asking “Why?” and “How Might We?” are game-changers in Design Thinking. They help you avoid quick fixes and instead focus on meaningful, innovative solutions. Keep these questions in your back pocket—they’re tools you can use for any challenge life throws at you!

 

Section 3- Narrowing Down Issues to Actionable Challenges

At this point, you’ve gathered insights, framed initial problem statements, and dug deeper with “Why?” and “How Might We?” questions. But sometimes, the problems you uncover can feel overwhelming or too broad to tackle. That’s where narrowing down issues to actionable challenges comes in. This step is about taking big, vague problems and focusing on specific, manageable pieces that you can realistically address. As a high schooler, this skill will help you break down complex issues—whether it’s a school project or a personal goal—into something you can actually work on.

 

Why Narrowing Down Matters: Broad problems like “The school cafeteria is a mess” or “Teens in my community are bored” are hard to solve because they’re too general. They include many smaller issues, and trying to fix everything at once can leave you stuck. Narrowing down helps you zoom in on one specific aspect of the problem that’s both important to users and doable for you to tackle. It turns a giant mountain into a climbable hill.

 

How to Narrow Down Issues: Here’s a step-by-step guide to focus your problem into an actionable challenge:

  • List All Related Issues: Start with your broad problem and brainstorm all the smaller issues or pain points connected to it. For example, if the broad problem is “The school cafeteria is a mess,” smaller issues might include long lines, not enough seating, unhealthy food options, and trash everywhere.
  • Prioritize Based on Impact: Look at your list and think about which issue affects the most people or causes the most frustration. Use your empathy data from Chapter 2—did students mention long lines the most in surveys? Does not having enough seats lead to the strongest emotions? Pick the one with the biggest impact.
  • Consider Feasibility: Think about what you can realistically address given your time, resources, and skills as a high school student. Solving unhealthy food options might require big changes to school policy (hard to do quickly), but addressing long lines might be something you can brainstorm solutions for now.
  • Reframe as a Specific Challenge: Take the narrowed-down issue and turn it into a focused problem statement or HMW question. For long lines, you might say, “Students need a faster way to get through cafeteria lines during lunch because waiting cuts into their break time.”
  • Check with Users: If possible, ask a few people (like classmates) if this specific challenge resonates with them. Does it match their experience? This ensures you’re not narrowing down to something irrelevant.

    •  

Example in Action:

  • Broad Problem: “Teens in my community have nothing to do after school.”
  • List of Issues: No safe hangout spots, expensive activities, lack of teen-friendly events, no transportation to existing programs.
  • Prioritize by Impact: Surveys show most teens mention “no safe hangout spots” as their biggest frustration because they feel bored or unsafe wandering around.
  • Consider Feasibility: Creating a new community center might be too big, but finding an existing space (like a library) for teen hangouts feels doable.
  • Specific Challenge: “How might we create a safe after-school hangout spot for teens in the community library so they have a place to relax without cost?”

    •  

Activity for Practice: Think of a broad issue at your school or in your community (like “School events aren’t well-attended” or “My neighbourhood isn’t teen-friendly”). Write down the broad problem, then list 3-5 smaller issues connected to it. Pick one based on impact and feasibility, and reframe it as a specific HMW question or problem statement. Discuss with a partner to see if they agree with your focus.

Narrowing down turns overwhelming problems into actionable challenges you can actually tackle. It’s about working smarter, not harder—focusing your energy on a piece of the puzzle that makes a real difference. This step keeps your Design Thinking project moving forward without getting bogged down by “too much to fix.”

As you narrow down your problem and start shaping a clear focus, there’s a sneaky trap to watch out for: assumptions. Assumptions are ideas or beliefs you hold about a problem or user without checking if they’re true.     •

  • Ask a Small Group of Peers: Talk to 3-5 classmates, friends, or others who are part of the user group (or know the issue). Keep it casual—say, “I’m working on a project and want your thoughts. Does this problem feel real to you?”
  • Ask Specific Questions: Don’t just ask, “Do you agree?” Dig deeper with:
    • “Have you experienced this issue yourself? Can you tell me about it?”
    • “Is this the biggest frustration for you, or is there something else?”
    • “Does this problem statement capture what you’re feeling?”
  • Listen Without Defending: If they disagree or point out something new, don’t argue—listen. Their feedback might show you’ve made an assumption or missed a key pain point.
  • Adjust if Needed: If multiple peers say the problem isn’t quite right, revisit your empathy data or ask more “Why?” questions to refine it. For instance, if they say long lines aren’t the issue but messy payment systems are, update your focus.

    •  

Example in Action:

  • Validation with Peers: You ask five classmates. Three say noise isn’t a big deal—they wear headphones. Two mention the real issue is not enough tables during finals.
  • Adjustment: Based on feedback, you revise to: “How might we provide more study tables in the library during finals so students have space to work?” This pivot ensures you’re solving a real, shared problem, not an assumed one.

Ask them if it feels like a real issue and if there’s anything you’re missing. Write down their feedback and note if you need to adjust your problem focus. Example: If your HMW is about hallway crowding and they say the bigger issue is locker placement, consider tweaking your statement.

Avoiding assumptions by validating with peers keeps your Design Thinking process honest and user-centered. It’s a quick reality check that saves you from wasting time on the wrong problem. Plus, it builds collaboration skills—asking for input shows you value others’ perspectives, which is huge in school and beyond!

Chapter 4: Ideation – Brainstorming Creative Solutions

Introduction: Unleashing Your Inner Innovator

Welcome, high schoolers, to Chapter 4 of your Design Thinking journey! After defining a clear and specific problem in Chapter 3, you’re now ready to dive into one of the most exciting stages: Ideation. This is where creativity takes center stage, and you get to dream up all kinds of solutions to the problem you’ve identified. Think of this chapter as your playground—there are no wrong answers, no limits to what you can imagine, and no idea too wild to explore. Whether you’re solving a school issue, a community challenge, or a personal goal, ideation is your chance to think big and let your imagination run free.

Ideation is the third stage of Design Thinking, and it’s all about generating as many ideas as possible to address the problem statement you crafted. In this chapter, we’ll explore what ideation really means and how to unleash your creativity without holding back. You’ll learn powerful brainstorming techniques like Mind Mapping, SCAMPER, and Crazy 8s to spark inspiration. We’ll encourage you to focus on quantity over quality by embracing wild, out-of-the-box ideas, and show you how collaborating with a team can bring diverse perspectives to the table. Finally, we’ll guide you through selecting the best ideas using voting and prioritization methods, so you’re ready to move into prototyping. Get ready to have fun, think differently, and discover that you’re full of amazing ideas just waiting to come to life. Let’s jump into the world of ideation and start creating solutions that can change the game!

Chapter 4: Ideation – Brainstorming Creative Solutions

 

Section 1- What is Ideation? Unleashing Creativity Without Limits

Let’s kick off by understanding what Ideation is and why it’s such a crucial part of Design Thinking. Ideation is the stage where you brainstorm and generate a wide range of potential solutions to the problem you defined in Chapter 3. It’s about coming up with as many ideas as you can—big, small, practical, or completely crazy—without worrying about whether they’re “good” or “possible” just yet. The goal is to explore every corner of your imagination and open up possibilities you might not have considered before. As a high school student, this is your chance to think like an inventor, artist, or dreamer, and apply that creativity to real-world challenges.

 

Why Ideation Matters: Ideation is the bridge between identifying a problem and creating a solution. Without this stage, you might jump to the first obvious fix and miss out on innovative, game-changing ideas. For example, if your problem statement is “Freshmen need a quicker way to pay for lunch because long lines cut into their break time,” ideation lets you brainstorm everything from a new payment app to a pre-order system to a completely reimagined cafeteria setup. By thinking broadly at this stage, you increase your chances of finding a solution that’s not just okay, but truly awesome. Plus, ideation builds skills like creative thinking and problem-solving that you can use in school projects, future careers, or even personal hobbies.

 

Key Principles of Ideation: Here are a few core ideas to keep in mind as you dive into this stage:

  • No Judgment: During ideation, there’s no such thing as a “bad” idea. Don’t criticize your own thoughts or anyone else’s—every idea is a stepping stone to something better.
  • Quantity Over Quality (For Now): Focus on generating lots of ideas rather than perfect ones. The more ideas you have, the more likely you are to stumble on something unique.
  • Build on Others’ Ideas: If you’re working in a team, listen to your peers and add to their suggestions with “Yes, and…” instead of “No, but…” This keeps the energy positive and collaborative.
  • Think Outside the Box: Don’t limit yourself to what’s realistic or easy. Imagine there are no rules, no budget constraints, and no limits to technology or resources. What would you create?
  • User-Centered Focus: Keep your problem statement and the user’s needs in mind. Every idea should somehow connect back to solving the challenge for the specific group you identified.

    •  

How Ideation Works in Practice: Ideation usually starts with your problem statement or “How Might We?” (HMW) question from Chapter 3 as your guide. For instance, if your HMW question is “How might we speed up cafeteria lines so freshmen have more time to eat during lunch?” you’d brainstorm any and all ways to address that need. Ideas might range from practical (a faster payment system) to wild (a robot server handing out food). You can ideate alone or in a group, using structured techniques (which we’ll cover next) or just free-flowing thoughts. The key is to let creativity flow without overthinking.

Example in Action:

  • Problem Statement: “High school athletes need more accessible storage for sports gear because cramped lockers cause frustration before practice.”
  • Ideation Goal: Come up with 20+ ways to solve this, like portable gear carts, expandable lockers, a gear-sharing app, or even a futuristic drone that delivers equipment to the field. No idea is off-limits!

    •  

Activity for Practice: Grab a piece of paper and set a timer for 5 minutes. Write down your problem statement or HMW question from Chapter 3 (or create a simple one, like “Students need a way to stay organized”). Brainstorm as many solutions as you can, no matter how silly or impossible they seem. Aim for at least 10 ideas. When the timer’s up, look at your list—did any surprise you? Share one wild idea with a friend and see what they think.

Ideation is all about unleashing creativity without limits. It’s a safe space to dream big and explore what’s possible, setting the stage for innovative solutions. As a high schooler, this process can help you see that your imagination is a powerful tool for solving problems in ways no one else has thought of. Let’s keep that creative energy going as we explore specific brainstorming techniques next!

 

Section 2- Brainstorming Techniques: Mind Mapping, SCAMPER, and Crazy 8s

Now that you understand what ideation is, let’s dive into some specific brainstorming techniques to help you generate tons of ideas. These methods are like tools in your creativity toolkit—they give structure to your thinking and help spark inspiration when you’re feeling stuck. We’ll explore three popular techniques that are perfect for high school students: Mind Mapping, SCAMPER, and Crazy 8s. Each one offers a different way to approach your problem statement or HMW question, ensuring you come up with diverse and innovative solutions.

  • 1. Mind Mapping – Visualizing Connections: Mind Mapping is a visual brainstorming tool that helps you organize thoughts and explore related ideas around a central theme. It’s great for seeing how different concepts connect and for sparking new directions.
  • How It Works:
    • Write your problem statement or HMW question in the center of a blank page (e.g., “How might we speed up cafeteria lines?”). Draw a circle around it.
    • Branch out with main categories or themes related to the problem (like “Technology,” “Layout,” “Payment,” “Timing”). Draw lines connecting these to the center.
    • For each category, add smaller branches with specific ideas or subtopics (under “Technology,” you might write “Mobile app,” “QR codes,” “Digital tickets”).
    • Keep branching with more details or related thoughts as they come to you. Use colors, doodles, or symbols to make it fun and engaging.
  • Why It’s Useful: Mind Mapping helps you see the big picture and uncover connections you might miss in a linear list. It’s perfect for visual learners and group brainstorming.
  • Example: For cafeteria lines, a branch under “Layout” might lead to “Separate lines for hot/cold food,” which could spark “Pre-packaged grab-and-go meals.”
  • Tip for High Schoolers: Use Mind Mapping for school projects or studying too—it’s a great way to brainstorm essay topics or connect historical events.
  • 2. SCAMPER – Remixing Existing Ideas: SCAMPER is a creative thinking technique that stands for Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, and Reverse. It prompts you to tweak existing ideas or systems to create new solutions.
  • How It Works: Take your problem or an existing solution and ask questions based on each SCAMPER letter:
    • Substitute: What can I replace to make this better? (e.g., “Replace cash payments with a card swipe system for cafeteria lines.”)
    • Combine: What can I merge to improve it? (“Combine lunch orders with a school app for pre-ordering.”)
    • Adapt: How can I adjust this for my context? (“Adapt a fast-food drive-thru model for school lunch pickup.”)
    • Modify: How can I change the size, shape, or process? (“Modify the cafeteria layout for multiple entry points.”)
    • Put to Another Use: Can this be used differently? (“Use library study rooms as overflow seating during lunch.”)
    • Eliminate: What can I remove to simplify? (“Eliminate long wait times by cutting unnecessary menu options.”)
    • Reverse: What if I flip the process? (“Reverse the flow—students pick food first, then pay at the end.”)
  • Why It’s Useful: SCAMPER forces you to look at a problem from different angles and rethink what’s already there. It’s awesome when you’re stuck or want to innovate on something familiar.
  • Example: For gear storage, “Eliminate” might lead to “Remove lockers entirely and use a shared gear room with sign-outs.”
  • Tip for High Schoolers: Try SCAMPER on everyday objects (like a backpack) to practice creative thinking—it’s a fun way to build this skill.
  • 3. Crazy 8s – Rapid Idea Generation: Crazy 8s is a fast-paced sketching exercise to generate lots of ideas in a short time. It’s perfect for visual thinkers and for pushing past mental blocks.
  • How It Works:
    • Take a piece of paper and fold it into 8 sections (or draw 8 boxes).
    • Set a timer for 8 minutes.
    • Sketch one idea per box to solve your problem—spend just 1 minute per idea. Don’t overthink; draw quick concepts (stick figures and shapes are fine).
    • Focus on variety—make each idea different from the last.
  • Why It’s Useful: Crazy 8s gets you to churn out ideas quickly without judging them. The time pressure helps silence your inner critic and boosts creativity.
  • Example: For cafeteria lines, sketches might include a conveyor belt for food, a ticket system, a student-led “express line,” or a food truck outside.
  • Tip for High Schoolers: You don’t need to be an artist—simple doodles work. Use this when you’re short on time but need a burst of ideas.

Activity for Practice: Pick one of these techniques (Mind Mapping, SCAMPER, or Crazy 8s) and apply it to your problem statement or HMW question from Chapter 3 (or a new one, like “How might we make homework less stressful?”). Spend 10-15 minutes on it. If you’re in a group, try one together. Afterward, write down 2-3 favorite ideas you came up with and why they stand out to you. Share with a classmate for feedback.

These brainstorming techniques—Mind Mapping, SCAMPER, and Crazy 8s—are powerful ways to fuel your ideation process. They help you think visually, remix ideas, and generate solutions fast, ensuring you don’t get stuck on just one way of solving a problem. Experiment with all three to find which works best for you, and remember: the goal is to let creativity flow without limits!

 

 

Section 3- Encouraging Wild Ideas: Quantity Over Quality

One of the most important mindsets in the ideation stage is to focus on quantity over quality and to encourage wild ideas. This might sound counterintuitive—aren’t we supposed to aim for the best solutions? Not yet! During ideation, the goal isn’t to perfect your ideas but to generate as many as possible, including ones that seem far-fetched, impractical, or downright crazy. As a high school student, this approach frees you from the pressure of “getting it right” and lets you tap into your boldest, most creative thoughts to solve problems in unexpected ways.

Why Focus on Quantity Over Quality?

  • More Ideas, More Possibilities: The more ideas you brainstorm, the higher the chance you’ll stumble on something truly innovative. Even “bad” ideas can spark a better one later.
  • Breaking Mental Barriers: Worrying about quality early on can stop you from thinking freely. Focusing on quantity pushes you past fear of failure or judgment.
  • Wild Ideas Lead to Innovation: Crazy, unrealistic ideas often inspire practical solutions. For example, imagining “a flying cafeteria” might lead to a more doable idea like “mobile food carts.”
  • Building Confidence: Generating lots of ideas shows you that creativity isn’t about being perfect—it’s about exploring. This builds your confidence as a problem-solver.

What Are Wild Ideas and Why Do They Matter? Wild ideas are solutions that ignore real-world constraints like budget, technology, or rules. They’re the “what if” thoughts that seem impossible—like “What if we had a robot teacher for every student?” or “What if the school bus was a teleportation device?” They matter because:

  • They stretch your imagination and push you to think beyond the obvious.
  • They can be toned down into feasible solutions (a robot teacher might become a personalized learning app).
  • They make brainstorming fun and energizing, especially in teams, keeping everyone engaged.

    •  

How to Encourage Wild Ideas: Here are some tips to embrace quantity and wildness in your ideation sessions:

  • Set a High Goal: Challenge yourself or your team to come up with 20, 30, or even 50 ideas in a short time (like 10 minutes). Don’t stop until you hit the number.
  • Ban Criticism: Make a rule—no one can say “That won’t work” or “That’s stupid” during brainstorming. Every idea is welcome.
  • Use Prompts for Wildness: Ask questions like “What if money wasn’t an issue?” “What if we lived in a sci-fi world?” or “What’s the weirdest way to solve this?”
  • Build on Ideas: If someone suggests a wild idea, add to it with “Yes, and…” For example, if a teammate says, “What if we had floating lockers?” you might add, “Yes, and they could follow students to class!”
  • Laugh and Have Fun: Wild ideas often lead to laughter, and that’s a good thing! A positive vibe keeps creativity flowing.

    •  

Example in Action:

  • Problem Statement: “High school athletes need more accessible storage for sports gear because cramped lockers cause frustration.”
  • Wild Ideas: “What if gear was stored in a giant inflatable bubble that pops up on the field?” “What if drones delivered gear to each player?” “What if uniforms were made of shape-shifting fabric that appears when needed?”
  • Toning Down: The drone idea might inspire a more realistic “gear delivery cart system” managed by student volunteers.

    •  

Activity for Practice: Take your problem statement or HMW question and set a timer for 10 minutes. Brainstorm at least 20 ideas, aiming for at least 5 to be completely wild (ignore all real-world limits). Write them down without stopping to judge. Afterward, circle one wild idea and think of a way to make it more practical. Share with a friend or group and see if they can build on it with “Yes, and…”

Encouraging wild ideas and focusing on quantity over quality is the heart of ideation. It’s about giving yourself permission to dream without limits and trusting that even the craziest thoughts can lead to brilliant solutions. As a high schooler, this mindset can help you tackle challenges with confidence and originality—skills that will shine in any project or future career. Let’s keep that creative energy alive as we explore teamwork next!

 

 

Section 4- Collaborating in Teams for Diverse Perspectives

Ideation isn’t just a solo activity—it’s often at its best when done in teams. Collaborating with others brings diverse perspectives to the table, helping you generate more ideas and see your problem from angles you might not have considered on your own. As a high school student, working in teams during ideation teaches you valuable skills like communication, listening, and combining strengths—skills that are useful in group projects, extracurriculars, and beyond. In this section, we’ll explore why team collaboration matters in Design Thinking and how to make the most of it during brainstorming.

Why Collaborate in Teams During Ideation?

  • Diverse Perspectives Spark Better Ideas: Everyone has unique experiences, backgrounds, and ways of thinking. A teammate might see a solution you’d never imagine because of their different viewpoint. For example, if you’re brainstorming ways to improve school events, someone who’s shy might suggest ideas for introverts that an outgoing person wouldn’t think of.
  • Building on Ideas: Teams can use the “Yes, and…” approach to expand on each other’s thoughts, turning a simple idea into something extraordinary. Collaboration creates a snowball effect of creativity.
  • Shared Energy and Motivation: Brainstorming with others is often more fun and energizing than doing it alone. A lively group can keep ideas flowing even when you’re feeling stuck.
  • Real-World Skill: Working in teams mirrors how many innovations happen in the real world—through collaboration. Learning to ideate together prepares you for future group work in college or jobs.

    •  

How to Collaborate Effectively in Teams: Here are some tips to ensure your team ideation sessions are productive and inclusive:

  • Start with the Problem Statement: Make sure everyone understands the problem statement or HMW question from Chapter 3. Write it on a whiteboard or paper where everyone can see it to stay focused.
  • Set Ground Rules: Agree on rules like “No judgment,” “Quantity over quality,” and “Everyone contributes.” This creates a safe space for sharing ideas, even wild ones.
  • Encourage Equal Participation: Make sure quieter team members have a chance to speak. Go around in a circle for one round of ideas, or use sticky notes so everyone can write thoughts anonymously if they’re shy.
  • Use Brainstorming Techniques Together: Try methods like Mind Mapping or Crazy 8s as a group. For Mind Mapping, one person can draw while others shout out branches. For Crazy 8s, everyone sketches individually, then shares.
  • Build on Ideas with “Yes, and…”: When someone shares an idea, others should add to it rather than criticize. For example, if a teammate says, “What if we had a school app for lunch orders?” you might say, “Yes, and it could let you customize meals in advance!”
  • Celebrate Diversity: Value different perspectives—someone’s cultural background, hobbies, or personal challenges might lead to a unique solution. Ask questions like “What’s something you’ve experienced that could help solve this?”
  • Keep It Fun: Use humour, draw silly ideas, or play music to keep the mood light. A positive vibe helps creativity flow.

    •  

     

Example in Action:

  • Problem Statement: “Freshmen need a quicker way to pay for lunch because long lines cut into their break time.”
  • Team Ideation: A group of four students brainstorms. One, who’s tech-savvy, suggests a payment app. Another, who works part-time at a fast-food place, builds on it with “Yes, and we could have a QR code system like at my job.” A third, who’s on the student council, adds, “Yes, and we could get volunteers to scan codes during peak hours.” A fourth, who’s shy but loves art, sketches a fun app interface. Together, their diverse perspectives create a richer idea than any one person could alone.

    •  

Activity for Practice: Form a small team (3-5 classmates or friends). Pick a problem statement or HMW question (from Chapter 3 or a new one, like “How might we make school hallways less crowded?”). Set a timer for 15 minutes and brainstorm as a group using one technique from the previous section (like Mind Mapping). Follow the “Yes, and…” rule and aim for at least 20 ideas. Afterward, write down one idea that came from someone else’s perspective that you wouldn’t have thought of alone, and reflect on how teamwork helped.

Collaborating in teams for diverse perspectives makes ideation more dynamic and effective. It’s about combining everyone’s unique strengths to create solutions that are richer and more inclusive. As a high schooler, mastering teamwork in this stage will not only help with Design Thinking projects but also prepare you for group challenges in any area of life. Now, let’s move on to narrowing down all those amazing ideas!

 

Section 5- Selecting the Best Ideas: Voting and Prioritization Methods

After generating a huge pool of ideas through brainstorming and collaboration, the next step in the ideation stage is selecting the best ideas to move forward with. You can’t prototype or test every single idea (at least not yet!), so you need a way to narrow down your list to the most promising ones. This doesn’t mean throwing out the wild ideas—sometimes they’re the most innovative—but it does mean focusing on solutions that best address your problem statement while being feasible and impactful. As a high school student, learning to prioritize ideas teaches you decision-making skills that are super useful for projects, time management, and even choosing future goals. Let’s explore some simple voting and prioritization methods to help you pick the winners.

 

Why Selecting Ideas Matters:

  • Focus Your Energy: You’ve got limited time and resources, so narrowing down helps you work on ideas with the highest potential rather than spreading yourself too thin.
  • Stay User-Centered: Prioritizing ensures you choose ideas that truly meet the needs of the user group from your problem statement, not just the ones you personally like.
  • Balance Creativity and Feasibility: This step lets you keep innovative ideas while considering what’s realistic to prototype and test in the next Design Thinking stages.
  • Build Team Consensus: If you’re working in a group, selecting ideas together ensures everyone agrees on the direction and feels invested in the next steps.

How to Select the Best Ideas: Here are three easy and effective methods to prioritize your brainstormed ideas. You can use one or combine them depending on your needs or team size.

  • 1. Dot Voting – Quick and Democratic: Dot Voting is a simple way to see which ideas have the most support, especially in teams.
  • How It Works:
    • Write or display all your ideas on a board, wall, or large paper (use sticky notes if you’ve got lots).
    • Give each person a set number of “dots” (stickers, marker dots, or checkmarks)—usually 3-5 per person.
    • Everyone places their dots on the ideas they think are the strongest. You can put all dots on one idea or spread them out.
    • Count the dots—the ideas with the most votes move forward (pick the top 2-3 depending on your project).
  • Why It’s Useful: It’s fast, visual, and lets everyone have a say without long debates. It’s great for groups of any size.
  • Example: For “speeding up cafeteria lines,” ideas like “QR code payment” (8 dots), “pre-order app” (6 dots), and “extra cashiers” (5 dots) might top the list.
  • Tip for High Schoolers: Use colourful stickers for fun, and do a quick “Why did you vote for this?” round to understand everyone’s reasoning.
  • 2. Impact vs. Feasibility Matrix – Balancing Creativity and Practicality: This method helps you evaluate ideas based on two key factors: how much impact they’ll have on the user and how feasible they are to implement.
  • How It Works:
    • Draw a 2x2 grid on a paper or board. Label the horizontal axis “Feasibility” (Low to High) and the vertical axis “Impact” (Low to High).
    • Place each idea in the grid based on:
      • Impact: Will this solve the user’s problem effectively? Does it address their core need?
      • Feasibility: Can this realistically be done with your time, skills, and resources?
    • Focus on ideas in the “High Impact, High Feasibility” quadrant (top right). If none are there, consider tweaking a “High Impact, Low Feasibility” idea to make it more doable.
  • Why It’s Useful: It helps balance wild creativity with real-world constraints, ensuring you pick ideas that are both impactful and possible.
  • Example: For gear storage, “portable gear carts” might be High Impact/High Feasibility, while “drones delivering gear” is High Impact/Low Feasibility (but could be adapted to a simpler delivery system).
  • Tip for High Schoolers: Keep it simple—use rough estimates for impact and feasibility. Discuss as a team if you’re unsure where to place an idea.
  • 3. Criteria Scoring – Detailed Evaluation: This method scores ideas against specific criteria to make a more structured decision.
  • How It Works:
    • List 3-5 criteria that matter for your project (e.g., “Meets User Need,” “Cost-Effective,” “Easy to Implement,” “Innovative,” “Scalable”).
    • List your top 5-10 ideas from brainstorming.
    • Score each idea from 1 (low) to 5 (high) for each criterion. Add up the total scores.
    • Choose the highest-scoring ideas (top 1-3) to move forward.
  • Why It’s Useful: It’s more thorough and helps you think critically about what makes an idea “best” for your specific problem. Good for solo work or small teams.
  • Example: For cafeteria lines, “pre-order app” might score high on “Meets User Need” (5) and “Innovative” (4) but lower on “Easy to Implement” (3), totaling 12. Compare to others to decide.
  • Tip for High Schoolers: Keep criteria focused on your user and project goals. Don’t overcomplicate—3 criteria might be enough.

Activity for Practice: Take the list of ideas you brainstormed earlier (or create a short list of 5-10 for your problem statement). Pick one of the methods above (Dot Voting, Impact vs. Feasibility Matrix, or Criteria Scoring) and apply it to narrow down to your top 2-3 ideas. If you’re in a group, do this together. Write down which ideas you chose and why the method helped you decide. Share with a classmate or teacher for feedback on your process.

Selecting the best ideas using voting and prioritization methods is the final step of the ideation stage. It helps you transition from a flood of creative possibilities to a focused set of solutions you can prototype and test in the next stage of Design Thinking. As a high schooler, mastering this skill teaches you how to make tough choices and focus on what matters most—a valuable lesson for any challenge you face. You’re ready to take your top ideas and bring them to life!

 

Chapter Wrap-up

Congratulations, everyone, on completing Chapter 4: Ideation – Brainstorming Creative Solutions! You’ve taken a giant leap in your Design Thinking journey by unleashing your creativity and generating a wealth of ideas to solve the problem you defined in Chapter 3. In this chapter, you’ve learned what ideation is and how to embrace a no-limits mindset, explored brainstorming techniques like Mind Mapping, SCAMPER, and Crazy 8s, encouraged wild ideas by focusing on quantity over quality, collaborated in teams to gain diverse perspectives, and selected the best ideas using voting and prioritization methods.

Ideation is all about dreaming big and exploring possibilities and you’ve built skills like creative thinking, teamwork, and decision-making that will serve you in school, personal projects, and beyond. Your top ideas are now ready to move into the next stage of Design Thinking: Prototyping, where you’ll turn concepts into tangible solutions to test and refine. Keep your problem statement and selected ideas close—they’re your guide as we dive into building and experimenting in Chapter 5. You’re doing incredible work—let’s keep the innovation rolling!
